title: Sanjaya remembers
hookLine: at the end of the Gita, the charioteer who heard it all keeps remembering it, and rejoices again and again
carry: reciting the gita again is itself worship

cards: The Bhagavad Gita doesn't end with Krishna's last word. It ends with two people remembering.
Arjuna speaks once more, briefly, and then the voice goes back to Sanjaya, the king's charioteer, who has been describing the whole conversation from far away.
Sanjaya says that as he remembers this dialogue, he rejoices, again and again. And as he remembers that form of Krishna, he is amazed, and rejoices again. A fitting close for a week of summit sits.

teach.b: Listen to what Arjuna says near the close of the eighteenth chapter, in paraphrase: my confusion is gone. Through your grace I have regained memory. I stand firm, my doubts are scattered.
I will do as you say. He doesn't say he has learned something new. He says memory has come back.
The word there is smriti, memory, and it carries weight in this tradition.
It's also the name for the great body of remembered texts, the epics and the Puranas among them. And just before that, Krishna says something about this very conversation.
In paraphrase: whoever studies this dialogue of ours worships me with the offering of knowledge, and whoever simply hears it with faith, without scoffing, is freed too.
That's the teaching, and it's why Hindu families and temples recite the Gita again and again: a chapter a day, the whole of it on Gita Jayanti, the same eighteen chapters for a lifetime.
In this tradition, going back over sacred words isn't review.

So look at this week from the top: a king who wouldn't leave a dog, a mother who saw the universe in her son's mouth, the saints singing at home, Ramana's question, a lotus leaf, a boy with one mantra. None of it was new.

teach.h: THE WHOLE WAY, AS ONE ROAD.
teach.b: All of it was remembered. And Sanjaya shows the last step. He doesn't remember once.
He keeps returning, and keeps being glad.

how: Many Hindus recite the Bhagavad Gita again and again, a chapter a day or the whole of it on Gita Jayanti, since the Gita itself calls studying it worship; the epics and Puranas are counted among the smriti, the remembered texts.

games.q: you are Arjuna. the long teaching is done, and Krishna asks whether your confusion is gone. what do you say?
o: my confusion is gone; I have regained memory.
I need more time to think.
games.why: Arjuna says his delusion is destroyed and he has regained memory, smriti, by Krishna's grace, and that he will do as Krishna says.

practice: Let the week walk back through you, one picture for each sit: a dog on a mountain road, a child's open mouth, a weaver singing at a loom, a question, water rolling off a leaf, a boy in the forest with one mantra.
Give each one a breath, then let them go and sit with whatever stays. If one of them makes you glad, let yourself be glad again, the way Sanjaya was.

wordCard.voice: Smriti. Memory, the word Arjuna uses when his confusion clears, and the name for the remembered texts, including the epics.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: smriti, memory; also the name for the remembered texts, including the epics.

carryVoice: Your line: reciting the Gita again is itself worship. Sanjaya rejoiced every time. Tomorrow, a goddess made of light. See you then.
